articles.title_orig: China's Communist Party seeks to tighten discipline
articles.title_zh: China's Communist Party seeks to tighten discipline
articles.content_orig:
Chinese President Xi Jinping, center left and Zhang Shengmin, Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission second from right attend a ceremony in honor of fallen national heroes at the Monument to the People's Heroes to mark Martyrs' Day at Tiananmen Square in Beijing, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — China's top leaders on Thursday elevated the only remaining general on the commission that oversees the country's military to the Politburo, the top governing body of the Communist Party.
The leaders also adopted a resolution on strengthening self-governance, discipline and anti-corruption in the party, as they seek to extend their grip on power.
During a four-day closed-door meeting, top Communist Party leaders deliberated on and adopted resolutions that will guide the party in the coming years. The meeting comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader.
The party elected Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who currently serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, to the Politburo. Xi had earlier purged two of China's top generals, leaving Zhang as the commission's only member besides Xi himself. It also left the Politburo without any representatives from the People's Liberation Army.
Zhang also holds a position overseeing internal discipline for the military, serving as deputy secretary of the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection.
The party said in a summary of the resolution that the tasks facing it were "increasingly arduous," such as "uniting and leading the people to safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."
It said it must step up its self-governance, which involves rooting out corruption and maintaining ideological purity.
The party should, "with an eye on enhancing its long-term governance capacity, maintain its progressive nature and purity, and its close, flesh-and-blood ties with the people," according to a summary of the resolution from the official Xinhua News Agency.
Xi has championed anti-corruption since coming to power in 2012, and has sustained a crackdown on officials for more than a decade. However, analysts say the focus now also includes underperforming officials.
Party members also reviewed the earlier purges of top members and military officials, confirming the personnel changes.
The plenum meeting revealed wider-than-expected purges, according to analysis by Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at Asia Policy who studies Chinese politics. He calculated an attendance rate of 74 percent, the lowest since the times of former leader Mao Zedong, who ran political purges regularly.

articles.title_orig: After losing his majority, Netanyahu tries to delegitimize election results
articles.title_zh: After losing his majority, Netanyahu tries to delegitimize election results
articles.content_orig:
Prime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majority
Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after he claimed that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to “steal” Tuesday’s election, in which the prime minister’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities in Israel , supposedly funded by foreign money.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the main opposition bloc, accused the prime minister and his Likud party of trying to derail the election results.
“It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,” Eisenkot said in a video message.
The prime minister’s allegations were quickly disowned by a range of government officials, including police officers and members of the election committee. Netanyahu was also rebuked by the president for “tarnishing an entire community”.
On Wednesday night, the prime minister posted a statement by Likud online , which described the claimed violations as “an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule”.
Tuesday’s elections led to Netanyahu’s far-right coalition losing its majority after four years in power. The main Jewish opposition bloc also fell short, however, leaving two Arab Israeli parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, holding the balance of power .
The prime minister’s attack appeared aimed at stopping the Jewish and Arab opposition voting together in the new Knesset to oust the incumbent speaker, Amir Ohana, a Likud politician and former Shin Bet official, and advancing their own legislation.
The Likud statement posted by Netanyahu on X said: “It is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra’am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel.”
Opposition leaders lambasted the claims of Netanyahu, 77, who has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.
Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. “Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,” Jabareen said, adding that he “refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided”.
Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted “without fear or favour,” and with “the utmost caution”, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.
The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.
The president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to “avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy”.
It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation. Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government “categorically” denied any involvement in the elections.
With almost all the votes counted, Netanyahu’s coalition has 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Eisenkot’s bloc has 48, and the Joint List and Ra’am together have 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.
The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist and openly racist members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.
On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.
Voting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.
Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far-right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.
The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist “Change” bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed the possibility of tactical voting in the Knesset to unseat Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.
One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.
Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told the Reuters news agency.
Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the “Change” bloc, pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling while the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are being accused of taking Qatari money for promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.
“This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,” Bennett wrote on X.

articles.title_orig: Greek container ship sinks after drone attack off Bulgaria
articles.title_zh: Greek container ship sinks after drone attack off Bulgaria
articles.content_orig:
The Greek-owned, Israeli-operated vessel sank off Bulgaria after being struck by three naval drones, as suspicions grow over Russian involvement in a wave of Black Sea shipping attacks
Israeli-operated cargo ship, the Contship Jet, was struck by unidentified naval drones in the Black Sea off Varna, Bulgaria, on Wednesday.
The Contship Jet, a Greek-owned, Israeli-operated cargo ship, departed Haifa on Sunday bound for Constanta, Romania, just north of where it sank.
The Bulgarian Navy said the ship was struck by three unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) at roughly noon local time, sinking hours later and taking 421 containers with it.
All crew members were rescued unharmed, ZIM announced.
Immediately following reports of the attack, French maritime patrol aircraft conducted reconnaissance missions in the area and supported rescue efforts.
The Contship Jet is the ninth civilian ship struck this month alone in the Black Sea, leaving over 30 sailors dead.
This attack comes as the defence ministers of Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey were meeting to discuss maritime security in the Black Sea.
Suspicion has fallen on Russia over the attacks, although Bulgaria’s government has been reluctant to assign blame.

articles.title_orig: At least 14 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.title_zh: At least 14 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.content_orig:
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least 19 people, including 14 at a busy platform in the main train station in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, officials said.
State rail company Ukrzaliznytsia said on Thursday that a jet-powered Russian drone hit the platform where a train was preparing to leave for the nearby city of Zaporizhzhia.
Regional Governor, Oleksandr Hanzha, said on Telegram that at least 14 others were injured and six were in critical condition, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denounced the attack as “horrific”.
“Just how many terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on certain Russian oligarchs and the Russian energy sector, rather than de-escalating?,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said Ukraine is experiencing a rise in attacks on its transport infrastructure.
“This marks a trend that we’ve seen lately here in Ukraine of Russian strikes targeting not only the country’s infrastructure, including energy installations, but also increasingly some of its transport logistics like railway stations and sometimes even those railways themselves,” MacAlpine said.
“Also, there has been a larger trend of mounting civilian casualties, according to UN human rights monitoring. Both Russia and Ukraine have seen their deadliest year of the war so far. This is all part of an upward trend that we’ve really noted here in Kyiv, with many, many attacks,” she added.
In Chernihiv in northern Ukraine, two teenagers were killed in a Russian attack on Thursday, while three people were killed in a separate strike on an apartment building in the central city of Kremenchuk.
Russia also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, damaging an educational institution, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram.
Russian news agencies, citing the Ministry of Defence, reported that its forces struck a cargo vessel used by the Ukrainian military in the Black Sea.
Meanwhile, Russia downed most of the 613 drones launched towards Moscow overnight, in a major attack on the Russian capital, state news agency TASS reported.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that air defence forces destroyed 231 of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) on approach to the city, with the remainder neutralised on distant approaches between Wednesday evening and Thursday morning.
The Kremlin condemned the attacks on Moscow as the city hosts more than 22 African leaders at a summit, TASS reported.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was “very strange” for Kyiv to target Moscow during this time.
The Russian Defence Ministry said its air defence intercepted and destroyed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight across regions.
Debris from downed drones also caused minor damage after falling onto the territory of an unnamed industrial facility in Sterlitamak, the second-largest city in Russia’s Bashkortostan region, Mayor Emil Shaimardanov said on Telegram.
He said the plant was operating as usual and that local air defence forces had shot down all eight Ukrainian drones involved in the attack.
The attack marks the latest in a series of major drone assaults targeting the Moscow region, following a record attack in September during which air defence forces reported shooting down more than 1,600 drones.
Both sides have reported an increase in attacks in recent months, while Moscow and Kyiv also prepare to resume peace talks next month with US mediation.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian delegation has headed to the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky, where a localised ceasefire is under way to provide humanitarian aid to the remaining residents.
The Kremlin also said it hopes aid will reach Oleshky on Thursday or Friday and that those wanting to leave the town were able to do so, Russia’s Interfax news agency reported.
So far, neither Ukraine nor Russia has reported any violations of the six-day ceasefire, which took effect early Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Villa Vie Odyssey passenger says warning signs were there long before Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Villa Vie Odyssey passenger says warning signs were there long before Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
A dream cruise around the world has come to an abrupt halt after two years at sea, reportedly leaving passengers scrambling to find somewhere to stay in Cambodia.
The Villa Vie Odyssey, a residential cruise ship that promised passengers the chance to make the ocean their permanent home, suspended its voyage Tuesday after its operator said soaring fuel costs had made it too expensive to continue.
CRUISE VACATION COMES TO CRASHING HALT AS SHIP SLAMS INTO 2 CARGO VESSELS
The ship was carrying 203 passengers, most of them Americans, and 156 crew members when it arrived in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, according to The Associated Press.
Passengers said they were given just seven hours' notice to leave the vessel Tuesday and had to make their own arrangements, despite the company's claims that it was helping residents find temporary accommodations.
In a statement, Villa Vie Residences, which is headquartered in Florida, announced that it had been "unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."
The company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin had climbed from roughly $1,800 to as much as $8,000 in parts of Asia.
ANGRY CRUISE PASSENGERS SAY FRUSTRATING ISSUE SHOULD HAVE BEEN DISCLOSED BEFORE BOOKING
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," the company said, according to the AP. "Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees."
The company added, "The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements. "
The ship first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024, on what was supposed to be a 3 1/2-year journey around the world.
For some passengers, the ship was supposed to be their permanent home long after the initial voyage ended.
MAJOR CRUISE LINE HIKES ITS POPULAR PACKAGE PRICES IN MOVE THAT COULD HIT VACATION BUDGETS
Fox Business reported in May 2024 that Villa Vie Residences was offering lifetime access to its Odyssey cruise ship through its "Endless Horizons" program for a one-time payment of $299,999 for a single-occupancy cabin or $499,999 for double occupancy.
At the time, the experience was billed as a budget-conscious alternative to traditional retirement.
The company marketed the program to retirees concerned about inflation, rising living expenses and the possibility of outliving their savings.
CEO Mikael Petterson similarly promoted the experience as a way for retirees to live on a fixed budget without worrying about ongoing expenses.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
"For less than the price of an average home, you can secure a lifetime of experiences," Petterson said at the time.
Speaking to AP, passengers expressed disappointment over the abrupt end to their voyage .
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming who boarded the ship 17 months ago, said they purchased a cabin with plans to spend years traveling the world — but were repeatedly asked to contribute more money for fuel.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," Lynn Montoya said.
"We had hopes, but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole," the AP reported.
California sisters Carol Larson, 69, and Crystal Lavering, 72, also said they were heartbroken after spending 18 months aboard the ship.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Larson, who paid $120,000 for her cabin, said she hoped residents could buy the ship and keep the cruise going.
Despite the setback, she told the AP she had no regrets about her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk," said Larson.
"From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth. … I still feel that way."

Fox News Digital reached out to Villa Vie Residences for comment.
The Associated Press contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Christine Lagarde to Step Down as President of European Central Bank
articles.title_zh: Christine Lagarde to Step Down as President of European Central Bank
articles.content_orig:
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said on Thursday she had decided to step down eight months before her term was due to expire so that she can speak more freely on issues beyond monetary policy.
Lagarde, 70, has led the ECB since November 2019 and previously headed the International Monetary Fund. Her term would otherwise have run until October 2027.
“There is never a good time to leave,” Lagarde told a press conference. “But it’s embedded in the governance of the ECB that presidents, board members have to leave because they cannot be up for renewal.”
Lagarde said the decision to leave early was driven by a wish to engage on issues outside the ECB’s mandate.
“I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters,” she said.
She noted that ECB officials are bound by strict rules of neutrality: “We have an obligation of neutrality, we comment on the situation with the focus on monetary policy,” Lagarde said, adding that the mandate is “the price we pay for being independent.”
Lagarde said she no longer felt comfortable staying silent on broader global issues. “I’m interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation,” she said, without elaborating.
Drawing on more than two decades in international economic and financial roles, Lagarde said she believed she had something to contribute beyond central banking. “There are things that I can say — whether people will listen or not is another story. But I feel that I should say those things and I cannot do so in my current position,” she said.
Lagarde sought to reassure markets and staff that her early departure would not disrupt the central bank’s operations. “A process has already started to identify my successor,” she said, adding there were “plenty of excellent candidates — much better than me, actually.”
She dismissed concerns about continuity. “Don’t worry about decision making in limbo — no, absolutely not,” Lagarde said. “The institution is solid, strong, like a rock, and it will continue being so.”

articles.title_orig: We're raising our price target on Eli Lilly as the obesity-drug boom rolls on
articles.title_zh: We're raising our price target on Eli Lilly as the obesity-drug boom rolls on
articles.content_orig:
As the commercial momentum behind Lilly’s tirzepatide franchise continues, analysts are increasingly turning their attention to new catalysts in the GLP-1 market, including the launch of oral obesity medicines and the recent rollout of a nationwide access program for seniors.
Since the summer debut of the GLP-1 Bridge program for Medicare Part D patients, Lilly executives have consistently pointed to the expanded access the program has offered seniors and the company’s early advantage over chief rival Novo Nordisk.
On Thursday, while detailing a 39% revenue jump for the third quarter, Lilly laid out additional details on how the new prescription pathway is expanding access to GLP-1 medicines.
As it stands, roughly “seven out of 10” seniors participating in the Bridge program are using a Lilly medicine, Ilya Yuffa, the company’s U.S. president, said on a Thursday call with analysts, noting that Lilly’s products have “performed really well” across the program so far.
The remaining share goes to Novo, with the two companies dominating the U.S. market for GLP-1 medicines used to treat diabetes and obesity.
While Lilly has gained a U.S. market advantage over Novo in injectable obesity treatments with its tirzepatide-based megablockbuster Zepbound, the competitive dynamics have shifted with the arrival of the companies’ oral GLP-1 medicines: Foundayo (orforglipron) for Lilly and the semaglutide-based Wegovy pill for Novo.
Analysts’ attention Thursday therefore turned to whether the Bridge program was moving the needle on Foundayo’s launch, which has lagged that of the Wegovy pill since its April debut, roughly three months after Novo’s oral medicine.
According to Yuffa, about 75% of patients entering the Bridge program are opting for injectables, a trend that may reflect the high efficacy bar set by Lilly’s own Zepbound, the executive suggested. Nevertheless, Lilly is witnessing “good growth and uptake of orals and Foundayo as well” through the Bridge, Yuffa said.
Foundayo generated $184 million in third-quarter sales. While the medicine continues to gain share in the oral obesity market, sales fell short of analysts’ expectations, the team at Citi wrote in a note to clients Thursday.
As for the Bridge program’s broader impact on GLP-1 use, Yuffa noted that about 80% of patients using the program are new to incretin therapies, describing what the company sees as a “significant driver of access long-term.”
Reflecting on Foundayo’s U.S. launch, “we’ve made significant progress since last quarter,” Yuffa pointed out on Thursday’s call, noting a recent uptick in consumer awareness thanks in part to a marketing campaign featuring Martha Stewart.
Yuffa said Lilly’s share of new prescriptions in the U.S. oral obesity market is approaching “four out of 10,” which he described as “good progress overall.”
Questions also surfaced during the call about Foundayo’s dose-escalation timeline, with Yuffa explaining that about 25% of patients have reached one of the drug’s maintenance doses, a proportion he suggested is “actually higher than what you see on the Wegovy pill.”
Lilly CEO Dave Ricks also pointed to the opportunity awaiting Foundayo in type 2 diabetes, which he said accounts for “roughly half the volume of GLP-1s” in the U.S. Novo also sells an oral diabetes medication under the Ozempic brand, a reformulated version of its semaglutide-based Rybelsus tablets. The product is distinct from Novo’s Wegovy pill for obesity.
Since its U.S. debut, Foundayo has expanded its reach this year with launches in the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia and Mexico, Patrik Jonsson, president of Lilly International, said.
So far, those international launches have also performed “very much in line with our expectations,” Jonsson said, adding that Lilly is seeing signs that oral GLP-1s are expanding the pool of patients receiving incretin therapies outside the U.S.
In January, Yuffa will step into the newly created role of president of Lilly Global Markets, assuming responsibility for both the U.S. and the company’s commercial operations abroad as Jonsson prepares to retire after 36 years with the drugmaker.
In the third quarter, Lilly generated $24.4 billion in revenue, representing a 39% year-over-year increase and coming in $1.8 billion above consensus projections, according to Citi analysts.
Unsurprisingly, Mounjaro for diabetes and Zepbound for obesity remained Lilly’s biggest growth drivers for the period, with Mounjaro generating $10.7 billion compared with Zepbound’s $5.4 billion. That represented year-over-year growth of 65% and 49%, respectively.
As Lilly maintains its lead in the broader U.S. GLP-1 market, Mounjaro’s sales also benefited from strong growth abroad, the Citi team pointed out. The analysts added that Mounjaro and Zepbound’s continued growth trajectories several years after their launches “remain impressive.”
Other significant contributors to third-quarter revenue included Jardiance, which delivered $1.6 billion, and Trulicity at $904 million. The Citi team said the two medicines collectively gave Lilly “additional cardiometabolic breadth.”
With its incretin business continuing to grow, Lilly raised its full-year revenue guidance to $91 billion to $92 billion, a $5.5 billion increase at the midpoint.

That was driven by US sales, which were up 7.7%, with roughly a 5% increase in ticket sizes as customers spent more at Starbucks and roughly a 2% increase in transactions.
"We have a clear plan. We've been working the plan. And the plan is working," CEO Brian Niccol said in prepared remarks. He added that the company is "operating with greater consistency" and that more customers are going to Starbucks.

articles.title_orig: Met refers itself to police watchdog over letter about Meghan's father
articles.title_zh: Met refers itself to police watchdog over letter about Meghan's father
articles.content_orig:
The Metropolitan Police has referred itself to the police complaints watchdog over its handling of a letter with allegations against Thomas Markle, which was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.
The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.
Markle has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".
The force said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) "in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex."
The Met added it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".
The letter that will be considered by the IOPC was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Roslyn Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.
The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".
Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason for not visiting Thomas Markle and not allowing him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.
Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".
Confirming that it had referred itself to the IPOC, the Metropolitan Police said it was aware of media reports that it had try to obtain a copy of the letter.
"While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," it said.
It added that the Met has carried out an initial review in recent days which has led to the voluntary referral to IOPC.
The watchdog will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas, it contained claims of alleged offences.
There are also reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to get a copy from the Sussexes.
Meghan, in a statement last week, said she believed the allegations in the letter "were being investigated".
But the watchdog will have to consider what happened to the warnings.
There are also likely to be questions about what royal officials knew about the letter, which was sent when Meghan was still a working royal, and which was forwarded to the Sussexes' office rather than to her personally.
Jim Gamble, former head of the Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre, previously told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he would have expected the police to have shared any warnings.
"If you get information that comes to you about someone from a foreign jurisdiction who represents a threat to children, there's a well-worn path and generally you'd expect a UK police force to share that information," said Gamble.
"I would have expected the Metropolitan Police to have gone to the FBI to say, 'Look, this isn't proven, it's an allegation, you might want to look at it'.
Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".
"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken, why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies," she said.
"I believe those questions deserve clear, transparent answers."
Reports of the Met's handline of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.
Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.
Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims.
Philippine Police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.
However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.
Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

articles.title_orig: Queen's Domain is a brilliant King's Field-alike RPG that forces you to walk so you can learn to fly
articles.title_zh: Queen's Domain is a brilliant King's Field-alike RPG that forces you to walk so you can learn to fly
articles.content_orig:
FromSoftware's elderly King's Field games aren't really celebrated for their feeling of agility. They are glorious first-person trudgefests, a treacle-thick waltz of swinging and spellcraft, with players wobbling in and out of attack range like British men who aren't sure whether the other man wants a hug. Unlike in the later Dark Souls action-RPGs, to which King's Field owes some of its retrospective popularity, there's no dodge-roll to grease the wheels.
Out this week on Steam, Queen's Domain is often as ponderous as King's Field, but it's also an exercise in steady, triumphant acceleration. Ultimately, it wants you to fly. To this end, it equips you - well, once you've boshed a huge skeleton sentinel - with a fancy windblade that lets you perform an aerial dash, speeding your manouevres while allowing you to reach new areas.
You'll find socketable gems that extend the dash, gradually bringing offshore islands and collapsed castle parapets within reach. I'm around four hours into Queen's Domain, and right now, the overall objective is tricking out that enchanted blade: heading down one leg of a marvellous, knotty world, retrieving a gem, and returning along another path, while keeping an eye out for nooks and platforms that once seemed like cordoned-off backdrop.
While an obvious quick-select default, the windblade doesn't make the 50 or so other weapons in the game obsolete, partly because enemies are distinguished by damage type: skellingtons are tougher against swords, while spears tend to bounce off malformed rodent ladybugs. All the weapons level up with use, and all of them have special abilities: the first spear you acquire has a retreating stab, useful against grasshopper chickens with lunging kicks, while the basic wooden club has a pounce move, skipping the lengthy swinging animation that is the weapon's major disadvantage.
For all these flourishes, combat is often as reassuringly stodgy as I remember King's Field being on the early PlayStation consoles. The pace is set by the need to charge your attacks, holding the button till the wind-up consumes your whole stamina bar; spamming blows is much less efficient.
350 words in, and I haven't mentioned the standout attraction in Queen's Domain – the landscape itself, an absurdly lovely expanse of mossy arches, chopped pillars and racked tombs that evokes Shadow of the Colossus and Vagrant Story as much as it does FromSoftware. It's a beautiful place, a haunting recovery of PS2 aesthetics that runs comfortably on integrated graphics. Or at least, it's beautiful until you start screwing around with focal length and lurid filters in the Photo Mode (see below).
The archipelago's interwoven paths are structured around save crystals where you can rest at the price of respawning enemies, but unlike in Souls, enemies eventually respawn of their own accord, appearing in different combinations as you pass certain milestones.
If this last wrinkle creates more potential for ambush, you can shape encounters using your secondary weapons, beginning with a belt of throwing daggers hanging from a shipwreck. I specify the location because embarrassingly, I managed to overlook them for the first hour – in general, Queen's Domain doesn't highlight collectible objects as flagrantly as certain recent blockbusters.
You get an endless supply of daggers, governed by a cooldown. The best thing about them initially is that you can use them to murder the highly annoying laser eyeballs that deck the tree trunks, often zapping you in the back while you're battling something else. Beyond that, you'll use them to bait individuals away from mobs, luring them towards killzones with plenty of strafing room, or getting them jammed behind monoliths so that you can bop their noggins at leisure.
I've got over 30 hours of Queen's Domain left to burn, according to devs Freshly Baked. Unlike with a lot of the non-review games I've dipped into this year, I feel like I might actually go the distance. More thoughts to follow, possibly! If you're new to King's Fieldalikes, you may find this stifling and frustrating at first. Even if you do know your King's Fields, you'll likely perish a lot. But hopefully, the landscape's magnificence and the increasing swagger of the combat system will get you over the hump. The game launches tomorrow, and there's still a demo on Steam as of writing .

articles.title_orig: Rep. Young Kim Urges Secretary Rubio to Raise China Travel Advisory to Level 3
articles.title_zh: Rep. Young Kim Urges Secretary Rubio to Raise China Travel Advisory to Level 3
articles.content_orig:
Oct 29, 2026 | Press Releases
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, House Foreign Affairs East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee Chair Young Kim (CA-40) sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging the State Department to raise its travel advisory for the People’s Republic of China (PRC) from Level 2 (“Exercise Increased Caution”) to Level 3 (“Reconsider Travel”) in light of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) ongoing wrongful detention of American citizens.
On October 19, the State Department updated its China travel advisory to warn that Americans face a serious risk of wrongful detention , arbitrary enforcement of local laws, surveillance, and illegitimate exit bans without due process. However, the advisory remains at Level 2 – the same category as allies like Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom, where risks stem from isolated non-state threats. In China, the threat to Americans comes from the state apparatus itself, making the risk constant and countrywide.
“The United States cannot and will not tolerate a hostile foreign power treating Americans, including Mr. Min Zin and Dr. Youlin Chen, who are currently detained, like pawns to be traded,” said Rep. Young Kim. “The Chinese Communist Party continues to use hostage diplomacy as leverage against our country, and Americans considering travel to China deserve a clear, honest assessment of the risks they face. Raising the advisory to Level 3 would deliver exactly that.”
Chairwoman Kim also urged that specific cases of detained Americans, like Mr. Min Zin and Dr. Youlin Chen, be listed on the State Department’s China travel advisory webpage as a warning to Americans.
This letter builds on Chairwoman Kim’s Subcommittee hearing, “Lives Not Leverage: The Long Arm of China and North Korea’s Repression,” where she pressed for answers on whether the State Department should raise China’s travel advisory.

articles.title_orig: Ancient cosmetics, coins, mouse skeletons found in Pompeii home shed light on life before deadly eruption
articles.title_zh: Ancient cosmetics, coins, mouse skeletons found in Pompeii home shed light on life before deadly eruption
articles.content_orig:
Ancient items found in a sealed closet in Pompeii hint at what life was like in the historic Roman city before it was destroyed in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in A.D. 79.
The closet was located in a home in the central area of the city, the Pompeii Archaeological Park said in a news release . The house had previously been excavated in 1912, but an investigation of the surrounding areas is just now underway.
Inside, archaeologists found cosmetics, an incense burner, a bronze lantern and a balsam jar. Weights, likely used for commercial activity, were also found inside a wooden chest of drawers. The researchers also found vases and pots made of materials such as bronze, glass and ceramic, and a "refined snuff bottle" decorated with pine.
A necklace representing multiple deities and made of several materials was also found. The piece of jewelry might have been considered "magical" during the Roman era, the park said. Now these pieces are known as "crepundia," or rattles. The necklaces have amulets, meant to protect the wearer as a child. Many carried them into adulthood as mementos of childhood, the park said.
There were high levels of "geographical mobility" in the Roman world, the archaeological park said, explaining that many people, from slaves to wealthy merchants, lived far from relatives and the places they were raised.
The necklace found in the closet contains at least 20 miniature objects and materials including bone and crystal.
The wardrobe also held 38 bronze coins, preserved in a container made of plant material. The presence of the coins has led researchers to believe that the owner or owners didn't have time to recover valuable items.
It's impossible to know what happened to the people who owned these items, the archaeological park said. They may have escaped the eruption of Vesuvius and been unable to return to the site and dig for their belongings. They may have died in the disaster, along with about 15% to 20% of Pompeii's population , or afterward, without heirs who could reclaim the objects.
Little is known about the residents of the house. The items in the closet, including the paintings, and the location of the home on one of Pompeii's main streets suggest "a certain standard of living." But mouse skeletons found inside the home cast some doubt on this belief. However, such skeletons have been found in other spots of Pompeii, showing the city contended with "unwelcome guests," the park said.
The home has previously been attributed to a person named Cornelius Maximus, the archaeological park said. That identification was based on the discovery of inscriptions that are no longer visible. The newly found items likely won't bring researchers closer to identifying the home's owner, but they allow archaeologists to study "the various traces of a life," said archaeological park director Gabriel Zuchtriegel in the Facebook post.
"We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of those who lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their daily lives," said Zuchtriegel.
Pompeii is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and popular tourist attraction. Archaeologists are also constantly exploring the ruined city, searching under heaps of volcanic ash and pumice to peer into its preserved remains.
In January, the archaeological park announced that researchers had found a 2,000-year-old love note and illustrated gladiator fight scene inscribed on a city wall. In December 2025, archaeologists found evidence suggesting that some Pompeii residents returned to live in the city after the eruption.

articles.title_orig: North Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise
articles.title_zh: North Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast into the Sea of Japan, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), less than a week after Seoul proposed talks over a growing border dispute.
The missiles were launched at about 12:30pm (03:30 GMT) on Thursday from an area around Wonsan on North Korea’s eastern coast, the JCS said in a statement.
Japan’s Defence Ministry separately confirmed the launch of what it said could be a ballistic missile that fell outside the country’s Exclusive Economic Zone, Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported.
The launch comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified border between the two Koreas, on September 21.
A joint South Korea-United Nations investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea had planted the landmines more than a year ago,with Seoul calling for an apology.
Pyongyang rejected the finding, sending a letter to the UN Security Council (UNSC) this week accusing Seoul of fabricating the explosion.
The North Korean permanent representative to the UN, Kim Song, wrote about the “provocation the ROK [Republic of Korea] committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious ‘mine explosion incident’”, warning that violations of the country’s sovereignty could trigger self-defence.
Song told the UNSC that South Korea’s claims were a “farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula”.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, labelled South Korean demands for an apology as “despicable” while separately rejecting an offer of medical equipment from Seoul.
South Korea has proposed military talks with its neighbour in a bid to calm the situation.
Seoul said last Friday that it had invited Pyongyang to discuss restoring communication channels. The offer was made as military activity on the border increases.
It remains unclear whether North Korea would agree to talks. Leader Kim has taken a hardline approach towards Seoul and suspended virtually all dialogue and cooperation with the South in recent years.
The ratcheting tensions come as United States President Donald Trump’s recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that US ally Seoul could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving the North.
Pyongyang launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested he might meet Kim this year.

articles.title_orig: China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
articles.title_zh: China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
articles.content_orig:
The top echelon of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) held a four-day session behind closed doors in Beijing this week, with the talks focusing on strict leadership and discipline inside the ruling party.
Xi Jinping , who is both the CCP's general secretary and the head of state in China , signaled he would not only deepen the existing anti-corruption effort , but also ensure that party officials demonstrate more loyalty and more initiative at all levels.
According to the press release published on Thursday, the committee published a resolution praising the leadership and Xi Jinping for "enormous political courage and strong sense of responsibility" in tackling the issues of corruption and the weakening of the Party's governance.
The statement emphasized the need to "consistently advance comprehensive and strict Party leadership."
Kerry Brown, head of the Lau China Institute at King's College London, says Xi wants to minimize potential sources of instability.
Amid the current international tensions and the internal problems in China, including economic difficulties, Xi is pursuing his anti-corruption campaign and by demanding loyalty . "This is just going to intensify because if [the CCP] isn't disciplined and united, the party believes that it will go the same way as everywhere else in the world at the moment and become disunited and unstable," Brown told DW.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Xi also recently spoke of the necessity to identify and remove "two-faced functionaries" from the political system.
In his speech, which was published in mid-October by the party's Qiushi Magazine, Xi referred to people professing loyalty to the central leadership while working against its instructions and following their own "individualistic" goals. The Chinese president described them as "political opportunists." He also criticized party officials pretending to be "nice guys," as in, those who use harmony as an excuse to stand aside when problems arise.
Brown points out that China's political system is now facing a crucial dilemma: If officials at all levels are now indeed expected to show innovation and courage in solving problems, the party's control could grow weak. This could, in turn, boost corruption.
However, if CCP leaders lean more on the "strict Party leadership" aspect and ramp up the pressure on the rank-and-file, there is also the danger of suppressing initiative. This could go beyond the party itself and could even affect the military.
The party is "very, very risk averse," Brown points out.
Chong Ja Ian, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore , notes that party functionaries under Xi only have a limited space to make their own decisions.
Taking this into account, the party's push for individuals to show initiative is not necessarily a major issue.
"I believe Xi would like for the officials to act proactively and decisively by conducting specific tasks; but he still doesn't want them thinking for themselves so much that they can question the agenda he prescribed. The 'proactivity' demanded by Xi is limited to the implementation, not decision-making," he told DW.
Brown adds that Xi seems to be ready to sacrifice a certain amount of operational flexibility to gain more control and stability.
"As long as you have unity, you live for another day, right? But if you have disunity, you probably die the same day," he told DW.
This approach "kind of works," at least at the moment, he added.
"It's not like the Chinese economy is disastrous. It's not great, but it's not disastrous. In any case, look at the outside world. It's a mess."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Outside observers are also focusing on Xi's future and possible successors for the 73-year-old leader .
For now, Xi seems to be firmly in control. It is highly likely that he would be confirmed as the party's general secretary next fall, and could stay in that position until 2032.
This is due to the changes pushed by Xi in 2018 , which removed term limits for state and party leaders.
Both analysts told DW that the issue of succession plays a major role in Xi's push towards internal stability.
"There's always a danger of differences in the party fragmenting it, especially when the question of succession comes up," says Brown. "And even though we don't expect to see a successor anytime soon, you know, there's going to be speculation about who might succeed Xi."
"He can't go on forever," he added.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Political scientist Chong Ja Ian says that Xi currently holds all the power. Therefore, the CCP leader could be afraid of his authority being undermined if he named a successor ahead of time.
"On the other hand, a failure to make preparations on time could create a power vacuum that can cause major instability," he told DW. "To solve this dilemma, the current leader needs to have both the necessary self-confidence and the readiness to take a step back — just like his predecessors did. But not everyone has that kind of confidence."

articles.title_orig: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it’s fixing that with more ads
articles.title_zh: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it’s fixing that with more ads
articles.content_orig:
In Alphabet's across-the-board earnings miss , one segment stood out above all else: search.
Revenue in the search and other segment grew 12% from a year ago to roughly $63 billion, but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. At the same time, Google said search query growth on the platform was the strongest it's been in five years.
The gap between usage and revenue within the search giant's flagship business is becoming harder to dismiss as more people turn to artificial intelligence bots and agents, including tools offered by Google. Since the early days of ChatGPT, analysts have predicted that traditional search will get eclipsed by AI, and warned that Google will have to figure out new ways to make money. While search remains a massive business, early signs of a shift are appearing.
"These things are going to be a force," Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster told CNBC's " Fast Money " after the earnings report, referring to new AI-powered services. Munster said that if "personalized bots" take off, "that will become for a lot of people the starting point of commerce, which impacts where Google is."
Alphabet executives said foreign exchange was the biggest factor behind the deceleration in search revenue in the period, and said the currency impact would be even greater in the fourth quarter.
The stock plummeted about 13% on Thursday, the steepest drop on record, reflecting the weaker-than-expected earnings report and negative free cash flow of $9 billion for the quarter, three times the estimated deficit. In the second quarter, Alphabet's free cash flow went negative for the first time in its history as a public company, at $5.9 billion.
Google has spent much of the past year telling investors that it needs to pour money into AI infrastructure and services to meet unending demand from consumers and businesses. Google's Gemini model has allowed the company to stay competitive with Anthropic and OpenAI , and its Gemini-powered enterprise services have proven to be a hit with customers.
The company also says that Gemini is strengthening its core digital ads business, as it uses AI to improve its ability to understand user intent and make advertising more relevant.
“We continue to accelerate the deployment of Gemini models across our entire ads infrastructure to boost performance,” Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said on the third-quarter earnings call.
The company made what Schindler called its “biggest update to product listing ads in a decade” during the third quarter, adding new AI capabilities.
“Overall, AI is accelerating our ads development and drives the majority of our product launches,” Schindler said.
Advertisers are also rapidly adopting AI tools. In the third quarter, Gemini models helped advertisers generate more than 1.5 billion campaign assets, up more than sevenfold from a year earlier, Schindler said.
But none of that addresses revenue growth for search, which slid from 19% in the first quarter to 17% in the second, before falling to 12% in the third.
Analysts at UBS wrote in a note that the results are "going to bring Search cannibalization fears right back to the forefront." And Mizuho analyst Jordan Klein said the numbers are an issue for search and YouTube.
"This elevates the fear around AI and agentic taking share from Search and YT and hurting their AI monetization narrative," Klein wrote in a note after the earnings report.
Where Alphabet's AI bet is very much paying off is in its cloud business.
Revenue in that division, which is racing to catch up to Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure, more than doubled in the quarter to nearly $31 billion. Cloud backlog also reached roughly $560 billion, reflecting enormous contracted demand for AI infrastructure. Management said it expects just more than half of that backlog to be recognized over the next 24 months.
In Microsoft's quarterly earnings report , which also landed after the bell Wednesday, the software maker said Azure revenue increased 48% from a year earlier to $33.2 billion.
Cloud demand is a big reason for Alphabet to keep spending.
The company maintained its full-year 2026 capital expenditure forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion and  said spending will increase significantly in 2027. Some of that is for its tensor processing units , or TPUs, which compete with Nvidia's graphics processing units. Alphabet just started selling them to outside customers in the second quarter.
Customer agreements first show up in Google Cloud’s backlog, and the company has to spend money building the systems before it can deliver them and recognize the associated revenue.
“You see cash going out and we’re building up the inventory base,” Alphabet CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the earnings call. “As we start delivering and billing customers for these TPU systems, then you see cash coming in.”
Still, Google has to contend with concerns about its longtime cash cow. Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, said the fears that existed from 2023 to 2025 about the AI effect appear to finally be showing up in Google's business.
"Investors will now worry that the miss in Search, YouTube and Subscription, leading to a profit miss, are an indication that AI has finally come for Google," Luria wrote in an email. "We would not rush to conclusions based on one quarter, but will definitely need to reassess what the world of agentic commerce means for Google."

articles.title_orig: China's PIPL at 5: Enforcement, evolution and what comes next
articles.title_zh: China's PIPL at 5: Enforcement, evolution and what comes next
articles.content_orig:
CIPP/E, CIPP/US, CIPM, FIP
Senior information governance officer
Beyond Change Advisory, Hong Kong China Network Security Association
In 2023, the fifth anniversary of the EU General Data Protection Regulation's implementation led to widespread reflection on its effectiveness, faults and international influence. The international cascade of regulations that followed the GDPR's introduction bolstered the idea of the Brussels effect, the phenomenon through which regulation within the European market influences global standards.
One of the most prominent examples is China's Personal Information Protection Law , which shares many of the GDPR's fundamental concepts. Effective 1 Nov. 2021, the PIPL now celebrates its fifth anniversary.
Comparable concepts include their respective principles, definitions of personal data and information and the roles and obligations of data handlers, the PIPL's equivalent to the GDPR's "controllers."
While these comparable approaches may make it easier for organizations to harmonize their operations, the two laws are not like-for-like. Among the most notable deviations is the Chinese approach to lawful bases. The PIPL does not contain an equivalent to Europe's "legitimate interests" basis, with consent relied upon far more heavily.
Now that the PIPL has had time to develop, the law's fifth anniversary provides its own opportunity for reflection on guidance and enforcement under the law to date.
Enforcement mainly comes under the remit of the Cyberspace Administration of China, though other authorities also contribute, primarily the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and Ministry of Public Security and certain sectoral regulators.
While landmark cases are handled by the CAC, enforcement actions involving mobile apps are often addressed by different authorities. Civil litigation has also emerged as a means for challenging unlawful processing, with multiple "guiding cases" now identified, providing greater clarity on specific PIPL compliance requirements.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Tankers strike mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says, as Hegseth fires top general
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Tankers strike mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says, as Hegseth fires top general
articles.content_orig:
Iran has not yet responded to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance to the secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to the semi-official Tasnim News agency, which is closely affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Tasnim said in a Thursday post on its official Telegram social media account that Tehran was not prepared to drop any of its core conditions for a ceasefire, which include lifting the American blockade of Iran's ports, easing sanctions and giving Iran access to its frozen financial assets held abroad, among other things.
Multiple news outlets have reported that Vance's letter to Rezaei was an attempt to restart peace negotiations, but President Trump said Wednesday that it was a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran's navy said a tanker it described as violating maritime restrictions was damaged and caught fire after striking sea mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the vessel unable to continue sailing.
In a statement, the navy said the incident occurred before noon on Thursday as the tanker was sailing through an area designated as prohibited and unsafe by Iran
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a shipping route in the south of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has insisted vessels can only use northern routes it has authorized.
The navy's statement warned that the Strait of Hormuz was closed "to violating vessels that, without coordination and relying on the lies of the U.S. president, intend to pass through prohibited and unsafe areas."
"These uncoordinated transits through high-risk areas have exposed and will continue to expose vessels and their crews to serious dangers," it added.
Qatar has categorically denied allegations of interfering in Israel's elections or funding efforts to influence their outcome, accusing Israeli politicians and media figures of launching a disinformation campaign to drag the small Persian Gulf state into domestic Israeli political disputes.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Majid al-Ansari said in a statement that Qatar would not be used as a scapegoat for Israeli politicians' failures, insisting that Doha had no involvement in Israel's political competition and would continue its mediation efforts between Iran and the U.S., as well as wider diplomatic engagement and support for the Palestinian people.
His comments come after Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu alleged that Tuesday's national elections were "stolen by Arab parties" and claimed foreign interference in the vote.
Israel's Shin Bet internal security service is investigating possible Qatari and Turkish funding used in an effort to influence the election outcome, according to reports by the Jerusalem Post and Israel's Channel 13.
"These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure," al-Ansari said. "The repeated invocation of Qatar in Israeli electoral rhetoric reveals an excessive obsession with our country among certain Israeli political and media figures."
Iran's navy has carried out more than 20 operations against U.S. warships and approximately 300 operations targeting American interests in various locations during the war, Iranian Army Navy Coordinating Deputy Rear Admiral Jalil Moghadam said in an interview published Thursday by the official state-run news agency IRNA .
Moghadam claimed the operations involved missiles and drones and said Iran's navy remains operational despite repeated claims by President Trump and other U.S. officials saying it has been destroyed.
"If the Iranian Navy has been destroyed, why have these forces not come closer than 500 or 600 kilometers to the Strait of Hormuz, or closer than 300 kilometers to our maritime borders? There is a force standing in their way, and that force must be the Navy," he said.
Moghadam did not offer any evidence to substantiate his claims.
IRGC spokesperson Brig. Gen. Abolfazl Mohebi challenged U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) to provide independent evidence for its claims of mine-clearing operations in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Prove your claim of mine-clearing in the Strait of Hormuz with independent evidence, not a statement!" demanded Mohebi in a post on X , adding that "the reality of the Strait of Hormuz is determined in the skies, on land and at sea — not on social media or in America's  media-warfare rooms."
Earlier Thursday the IRGC said three oil tankers had been disabled after striking mines in the strait, and the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center confirmed one vessel in the area was seen on fire.
In late August, President Trump and CENTCOM chief Adm. Brad Cooper insisted the primary shipping lanes of the Strait of Hormuz had been demined and were safe for commercial vessels.
In a statement posted online, Cooper said the U.S. military had "meticulously and quietly" cleared mines previously laid by the IRGC.
"Internationally recognized transit routes in the strait are free of Iranian sea mines thanks to the incredible work of the U.S. military," he said. "Today, international shipping lanes are open, and momentum is building."
Iran's Houthi allies said Thursday that a Saudi strike on a residential area in Yemen's western Taiz province killed 12 people, as the two sides continued to exchange fire in the reignited Yemeni civil war.
"As an initial toll, 12 citizens were killed and three others were critically injured when the Saudi enemy targeted the homes of the families of Ibrahim Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz and Al-Raabi Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz in Al-Barah, Maqbana district," the Houthi health ministry said in a statement shared by the group's Saba news agency.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in Yemen in July, months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis. The Saudis, who back Yemen's government, have engaged in fighting with the Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast and in deadly back-and-forth strikes.
Iran has used some 5,000 agencies to help it slip past the U.S. naval blockade to import hardware, explosives and trucks needed for its drone and missile programs over land, sea and air, according to a report by the Reuters news agency .
The secret network of military agencies has helped Iran usher at least $2 billion in components into the country since 2025, evading Western sanctions and, since earlier this year, the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels.
Some of the agencies are linked to Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), others to business conglomerates run by the country's elite, Reuters said.
Between January 2025 and June 2026, before the U.S. blockade was imposed but with myriad U.S. and international sanctions in place, a single company, MOD 346428, imported large quantities of rocket propellants, explosives and weapons parts crucial for drones and missile production, as well as trucks that can be used as missile launchers. The hardware was brought in from China, Russia and Germany, Reuters reported.
The agencies all use the address of Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics in Tehran. Most were established in 2013, when Iran was struggling under international sanctions, the investigation found.
Iran's Intelligence Ministry said Thursday that it had dismantled four alleged terrorist cells and arrested 16 suspects in the central and southern parts of Sistan and Baluchestan Province, while detaining three more individuals accused of gathering and transmitting information about security and defense sites in the country's southeast.
In a statement, the provincial intelligence directorate said the operations were carried out in recent days following public tips and ongoing intelligence and operational surveillance, in cooperation with other provincial security forces. It alleged that the cells were affiliated with terrorist groups linked to the United States and Israel.

articles.title_orig: Take a look inside the 'never-ending' Villa Vie Residences Odyssey cruise ship stranded in Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Take a look inside the 'never-ending' Villa Vie Residences Odyssey cruise ship stranded in Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
A US Cruise ship stranded in Cambodia in the midst of an around-the-world trip asked passengers for money to refuel, it has been claimed, as reports suggest crew members working on board the Odyssey still haven’t been paid.
Lynn Montoya, who is travelling on the three-year trip alongside her husband Paul, said residents on board the cruise ship were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a call to raise funds for fuel to leave Cambodia.
Lynn said crew members working on the ship had also not been paid amid a lack of funds and soaring fuel costs.
“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” she said. “We had hopes, but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement.”
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a trip intended to go around the world, with suite prices starting at around $230,000 (£172,000), but ran into trouble in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, after running out of fuel. For now, it remains docked in Cambodia with no certain departure date.
Guests were told at 6am on Monday that they had to disembark by 2pm that day. The cruise ship has capacity for 650 passengers, but 203 were on board - mostly Americans - when it suspended operations. There were also 156 crew members on board the ship.
Villa Vie Residences, the Florida-based operator of the MV Odyssey, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that used to average around $1,800 (£1352) , have skyrocketed to $6,000-$8,000 (£4,000-£6,000) in parts of Asia due to the ongoing war in Iran.
Traffic has largely been suspended in the Strait of Hormuz, an essential shipping lane transporting a vast proportion of the world’s oil, putting a major strain on fuel prices and sharply increasing costs - especially in Southeast Asia.
The cruise liner firm tried to decrease its fuel consumption by slowing down the itinerary and spending more time docked in port, but ultimately was unable to curb soaring fuel prices.
In a statement on Tuesday, Ville Vie Residences said: “We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.
“Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus is now supporting residents, crew and employees. The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements.”
Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin were among hundreds of guests who looked forward to a new life at sea when they boarded residential world cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey in October 2024.
The 56-year-olds sold a business to fund a $100,000 (£75,000) cabin on the ship – plus monthly maintenance fees of $3,500 (£2,633). Lanette ran a windshield-replacement company from the ship, and the pair documented their journey on their Living Life on a Cruise YouTube channel.
The couple said they knew leaving was possible because rumours had circulated on the ship about financial difficulties, but the eight-hour notice still surprised them.
Lanette said: “Our immediate reaction was a deep sense of heartbreak at having to leave the home and community we had built over the past two years.
“It was difficult to process the news while packing up our life and saying goodbye to the place we had come to love.”
She said Villa Vie helped unload suitcases and provided shuttles to and from the port, but it has not helped with paying for hotels.
Lanette said a fellow resident has offered to help others struggling financially with lodging costs and is working to arrange a charter flight to San Francisco.
She said: “Villa Vie has not given us a date for returning onboard. Regardless of whether operations resume, we have decided to move on. The company was planning to increase our maintenance fees, which would have priced us out.”
The couple now plan to stay at a hotel in Sihanoukville for about a week, then spend some time in Phnom Penh, and travel to Vietnam, Bali in Indonesia, and Thailand, where they hope the lower cost of living will help sustain their lifestyle while they figure out their longer-term plans.
Lanette said: “We’re doing well, considering everything, but we are heartbroken. There have been many hugs and tears. We loved our two years aboard, the adventures, the friendships, and especially the community. Many residents are settling together off the ship, so those connections are continuing on land.”
Other residents have complained about a lack of communication and support from the cruise line. One former resident, Sharon Lane , who had to leave the ship last year due to health issues, says her friends on board have been left confused.
She told The Independent : “There seems to be confusion as to what is being provided to residents.
“Communication has been an ongoing issue. I am very concerned for my friends. They need to figure out transport, visas, housing; it is very stressful. It took me weeks to arrange my departure, and they [only] had a few hours.”
Sharon still owns a cabin on the ship because her contract terms don’t let her rent it out, and a sale now looks unlikely.
She added: “I’ve lost money; everyone who owns has or will lose money. It is devastating for some who sold their own properties to fund this. It breaks my heart. I hope the owners of the ship keep the interests of the residents in mind.”
The Independent has contacted Villa Vie Residences for further comment.

articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a production facility in Japan to jointly manufacture advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles , according to the Japanese defense chief.
The decision marks the latest step by the two allies to bolster security capabilities amid heightened concerns over China 's growing military assertiveness across Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced the agreement during a news conference Wednesday evening in Cebu, a province in the central Philippines .
His remarks followed a bilateral meeting with U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual gathering of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
During a session on Thursday, Koizumi highlighted increased Chinese naval presence near southwestern Japan, noting that three Chinese destroyers alongside a coast guard vessel recently passed through the Osumi Strait south of Kyushu into the Pacific Ocean.
He stated that it was the first time his ministry had recorded such a fleet configuration.
Koizumi pointed to the transit as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region," adding that Tokyo will maintain close surveillance of Chinese naval operations while continuing to accelerate its own military buildup in southwestern Japan.
The annual meetings aim to prevent major conflict and deepen regional cooperation, though the U.S., China, and their respective allies frequently exchange criticisms during the proceedings.
The joint manufacturing effort, titled "Operation Supercharge," will establish a final assembly and inspection plant in Japan for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM.
Koizumi emphasized that these missiles are essential for F-35 stealth fighters, which are operated by both the U.S. and Japanese militaries.
Recounting his meeting with Hegseth, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."
He added: "We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means."
In a separate meeting with ASEAN defense ministers led by Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr., Hegseth offered renewed assurances regarding Washington's commitment to regional stability.
Without calling out Beijing by name, Hegseth outlined the U.S. approach.
"The approach we’re taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the defense chiefs, adding it is "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."
He emphasized that the position is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners."
Hegseth reassured the Philippines, Washington’s oldest treaty partner in Asia, that the Trump administration will maintain robust deterrence against Beijing’s actions in the South China Sea, a critical trade waterway claimed almost entirely by China.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles pledged that Australian forces, alongside allies like the U.S., would continue upholding international law despite Chinese actions in disputed waters.
Referring to an incident last year where a Chinese J-16 jet released flares near an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance plane, Marles said: "That doesn’t deter us from doing what we need to do and that’s essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific."
He added: "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."
Territorial claims in the South China Sea remain contested among the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, and Taiwan, with frequent standoffs involving Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval vessels.
Washington maintains that it is bound by treaty to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships, or aircraft come under armed attack. Separately, Tokyo and Beijing remain locked in a maritime dispute over Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea.

articles.title_orig: A rock formation collapse in Turkey’s touristic Cappadocia region kills at least 3
articles.title_zh: A rock formation collapse in Turkey’s touristic Cappadocia region kills at least 3
articles.content_orig:
Parts of a large volcanic rock formation crashed down in Turkey’s popular tourism destination of Cappadocia on Thursday, killing at least three people and injuring five others, officials said.
A section of the rock formation — known as a fairy chimney — tumbled in Cappadocia’s Goreme region, prompting authorities to deploy medical and rescue teams.
Gov. Huseyin Kok said recent heavy rains likely caused the collapse, which occurred near a parking lot at an entrance to the site.
He said rescue teams were continuing to search for other people who may be trapped under the debris.
“We hope that there are no other casualties,” the governor said. “We are deeply saddened.”
Kok said two of the three dead were Turkish nationals. He did not provide information on the third victim.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation was launched into the incident.
HaberTurk news channel showed heavy machinery removing chunks of rock from the foot of the formation.
Cappadocia, in central Turkey, is a UNESCO World Heritage-listed site famed for its distinctive rock formations and ancient underground cities. It is one of the country’s most visited tourism locations.
The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day holiday, when the area would have been crowded with visitors.
